identity.title: Asynchronous Service Execution
identity.mainTitle: OPC UA FOR ASYNCHRONOUS SERVICE EXECUTION
identity.subTitle: Part 1: Deferring and continuing a Service request
identity._comment_namespaceIsSubset: This document adds Nodes to the base OPC UA namespace rather than owning one, so its UANodeSet holds only those additions. Stating False here would claim the file contains the whole base namespace.
introduction: A Server cannot always answer a request in the time its Client is willing to wait. A gateway asked to distribute a TrustList to the devices behind it, an aggregating Server asked to write a value that lives elsewhere, a Server asked to run a Method that turns a machine: the work outlasts the request, and OPC UA has no way to say so.

What the Client gets today is a timeout, which does not distinguish a Server that failed from a Server that is still working. It therefore cannot safely retry: repeating a certificate update or a Method that moves an axis is not the same as repeating a read.

This document defines asynchronous Service execution, which is the missing answer. A Server that cannot respond in time parks the request and says so with a StatusCode that already exists for the purpose, together with a hint about when to ask again. A new Service, Continue, collects the response when it is ready, keyed on the request handle the Client already assigned and the Cancel Service already uses. It is a proposed addition to the base OPC UA namespace, not a new companion namespace.
identity.draftBanner: PROVISIONAL WORKING DRAFT — not normative, not endorsed by the OPC Foundation. The document number, the Mantis project identifier, the StatusCode values and every NodeId in this document are placeholders; the OPC Foundation assigns the real values.

_comment_useCases: The template requires a Use cases clause. This document's material of that shape is Annex B, a worked gateway deployment; this clause states the families of problem it belongs to.
useCases: Deferral is for a Service call whose answer may legitimately outlast the call. Three families of use case motivate it.

Gateways and aggregating Servers. A Server that fronts other devices or other Servers cannot answer faster than the slowest thing it has to reach. The certificate push Methods of OPC 10000-12 are the sharpest example — one call on the gateway becomes one exchange per device behind it — and Annex B works such a deployment through in full. The same shape appears whenever an aggregating Server forwards a Write or a Method call to an underlying Server.

Operations that change the physical world. A Method that moves an axis, runs a recipe or commissions a device takes as long as the equipment takes. Today a Client either holds a request open for the duration or loses track of the outcome; with a deferral it collects the result when the work is done, and the audit trail records the outcome whether or not it does.

Clients that cannot stay connected. A commissioning tool, a scheduled job or a cloud-hosted Client may not survive an hour-long operation. Durable deferral lets a later Session of the same user identity collect a response the Session that asked for it never saw.

Deferral is not a replacement for a Subscription, which reports what a Client did not ask for, nor for the ticket Methods that individual specifications already define, which continue to work unchanged. Annex C sets out which mechanism suits which shape of problem.
